system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2155-09-27 14:10:00 to 2155-09-30 15:48:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for recurrent nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Workup revealed gastroparesis confirmed by a gastric emptying study showing 85% retention at four hours, and a Campylobacter infection identified on stool culture. She was treated with azithromycin and restarted on metoclopramide at a reduced dose with improvement. A liver biopsy ruled out hepatic GVHD, allowing reduction of prednisone from 17.5 mg to 15 mg daily. Her tachycardia and lightheadedness improved with hydration. She tolerated oral intake, and symptoms resolved prior to discharge. She was discharged home on azithromycin, metoclopramide, prednisone, and continued anticoagulation, with plans for outpatient follow-up.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  CTA CHEST AND CT ABDOMEN AND PELVIS

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with hx recurring PE/DVT, CML ___ s/p allo
SCT, presents with pleuritic CP and increased bloating // any sign of clot or
infection?

TECHNIQUE:  Axial CT images of the pulmonary arterial phase. Subsequent venous
phase imaging of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained with intravenous and oral
contrast . Sagittal and coronal reformats were obtained.

DLP:  478 mGy-cm

COMPARISON:  CT Torso ___. MRCP ___.

FINDINGS: 

Appropriate opacification of the main pulmonary arteries and segmental
branches was obtained. There is no filling defect demonstrated. The pulmonary
arteries are normal caliber. The heart size is normal and there is no
pericardial effusion.

No mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy is demonstrated.  Calcified right and
left hilar, and left para-aortic lymph nodes are in keeping with prior
granulomatous infection.  6 mm densely calcified granuloma is noted in the
anterior basal segment of the right upper lobe, and there is a 2 mm
non-calcified pulmonary nodule in the right middle lobe (4,84).  8 mm rounded
calcification is noted in the right breast.

The IVC, hepatic veins, iliac, and common femoral veins are patent
bilaterally.  There is no hepatic lesion demonstrated. The patient has had
previous cholecystectomy. The spleen is normal size.

1.8 cm cystic lesion in the pancreatic head, and 8 mm lesion in the pancreatic
body are unchanged from the prior CT examination.  The adrenal glands and
kidneys are unremarkable.  There is no small or large bowel dilatation
present.  A few scattered sigmoid diverticula are noted. There is no abdominal
or pelvic lymphadenopathy.  The bladder is unremarkable.

Mild anterior vertebral wedging at T11 is unchanged from the prior exam. A new
compression fracture is demonstrated at L1 with moderate associated height
loss. Multiple old healed left rib fractures are noted.

IMPRESSION:


1. No pulmonary embolus.
2. No venous thrombosis seen within the abdomen or pelvis.
3. No features of active infection within the chest abdomen or pelvis.
4. L1 compression fracture with moderate height loss that has developed since
the prior exam
5. Pancreatic cystic lesions measuring up to 1.8cm in the pancreatic head
again in keeping with side branch IPMN are unchanged from the prior CT.

HISTORY:  Chronic steroids.

FINDINGS:  In comparison with the study of ___, there again is mild
degenerative change symmetrically involving both sides.  No evidence of
avascular necrosis.  If this is a serious clinical concern, given the steroid
use, MRI could be obtained.

EXAMINATION:  CT SINUS/MANDIBLE/MAXILLOFACIAL W/ CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman s/p allo sct with recent viral URI and
persisting congestion for 2 months  // any sign of infection

TECHNIQUE:  Helical axial MDCT images were acquired through the paranasal
sinuses. Coronal reformatted images were prepared.

DOSE:  CTDIvol:  37.10

DLP:  560.70

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to CT head dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

There is moderate mucosal thickening of the bilateral maxillary sinuses, more
significant on the right. Mucosal thickening is also seen within the left
sphenoid sinus, and the bilateral ethmoid air cells. Aerosolized secretions
are seen within the right frontal sinus. The left ostiomeatal unit is patent,
however, the right ostiomeatal unit is obscured by the adjacent lobulated
mucosal thickening of the right maxillary sinus. The cribriform plates are
intact. There is no evidence of bony sclerosis.

The anterior clinoid processes are not pneumatized. The lamina papyracea is
intact. The nasal septum is mildly deviated towards the left. The
temporomandibular joints are symmetric and unremarkable. The orbits and
nasopharyngeal soft tissues are unremarkable.

Allowing for helical acquisition, reconstruction algorithm, and section
thickness, the visualized brain is grossly unremarkable.

IMPRESSION: 

1. Aerosolized secretions within the right frontal sinus may represent acute
sinusitis. Recommend clinical correlation.

2. Diffuse, lobulated mucosal thickening of the bilateral maxillary sinuses
and left sphenoid sinus. Findings are suggestive of chronic sinus disease.

FOUR VIEWS OF BOTH SCAPULAE:  There is no scapular fracture.  The glenohumeral
and acromioclavicular joints are unremarkable bilaterally.  The lungs are
grossly normal, but better evaluated on the recent chest CTA.  Soft tissues
are unremarkable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having chest pain when you breathe in. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about a week ago. It hurts more when I take a deep breath. I also feel short of breath, but I can still do my daily activities.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of blood clots, we need to make sure this isn’t another pulmonary embolism. We’ll do a CT scan of your chest right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had several clots before. I’m on lovenox every day. Could it still happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, even with anticoagulants, there’s still a risk, especially with your medical history. But we’ll check thoroughly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Good news—there’s no blood clot in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did see a new compression fracture at L1 in your spine. That might be contributing, but it doesn’t fully explain the chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had several of those. But this pain is different—it’s sharp when I breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed old rib fractures. Sometimes those can cause lingering pain, especially with deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had so many fractures over the years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also concerned about infection or inflammation. You mentioned congestion and cough—have you had a cold recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about two months ago. The cough never really went away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get a CT of your sinuses to check for sinusitis. That could explain both the cough and the chest discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your sinus CT shows acute frontal sinusitis and chronic maxillary sinusitis. That’s likely contributing to your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s a sinus infection? I didn’t have a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not all infections cause fever, especially with your immune system changes from GVHD and steroids. We’ll start you on levaquin for 7 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will that help the chest pain too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help with the cough and congestion, which may reduce the strain on your chest. We’ll also keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been more bloated lately. My stomach feels full all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a history of gastroparesis. Are you still taking metoclopramide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, three times a day. But it doesn’t seem to be helping as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue it and add simethicone for gas. If bloating persists, we may need to see GI after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your CMV—it’s negative. That’s good, means no active viral infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had CMV before. I’m glad it’s not back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also tried a respiratory virus test, but the sample wasn’t adequate. We’ll repeat it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The repeat respiratory virus test came back negative. No flu, RSV, or other common viruses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a cold then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it looks like your symptoms are from the sinus infection, not a viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my back and hip pain? It’s been bothering me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did X-rays of your hips. There’s mild arthritis, but no avascular necrosis. Your back pain is likely from the fractures and degenerative changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on morphine and oxycodone. Is that still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep your current pain regimen. The lidocaine patch also seems to help your mid-back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye drops? I’ve been using them regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using the cyclosporine and autologous serum drops. Your eyes are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugar has been okay. I used to be on insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your A1C was 6.3—well controlled. Since your steroid dose is low, we’ll continue monitoring without medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your scapular pain. The X-ray showed no fracture. Likely referred pain from your spine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels better with the oxycodone. Should I see physical therapy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss that at your follow-up. For now, focus on healing from the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your chest pain has improved, and your oxygen levels are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the levaquin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish the 7-day course at home. Continue all your regular medications, including lovenox, prednisone, and metoclopramide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bloating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using simethicone. If it doesn’t improve, follow up with GI. It could be related to your gastroparesis or SIBO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting due to the L1 fracture. Use your pain meds as needed, and keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Call if you have any concerns before then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep using your albuterol and fluticasone inhalers for your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t been using them as much, but I’ll continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Even if you feel fine, they help prevent flare-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll stick to the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get you home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is here for you. Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you in clinic.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for pleuritic chest pain and concern for pulmonary embolism given her history of recurrent DVT/PE. CT angiography ruled out pulmonary embolism but revealed a new L1 compression fracture and chronic rib fractures. A CT of the sinuses showed acute frontal and chronic maxillary sinusitis, which was treated with levaquin. Her chest pain resolved during the admission. She also reported persistent bloating, attributed to her known gastroparesis, and was continued on metoclopramide and simethicone. Her chronic GVHD, diabetes, and pain from prior fractures were managed with her baseline medications. She remained stable, completed treatment, and was discharged home with follow-up plans.
